===============================================================================
RESIDENTIAL DWELLING INSURANCE
GENERAL POLICY CONDITIONS - PROPERTY DAMAGE COVER
Policy wording "WD-2026" - Water Escape, External Surfaces and Site Charges
Edition
Fictional mock document created for test purposes only. All wording is
invented. No real contract.
===============================================================================

These conditions apply together with the General Contract Provisions and with
the Schedule, both of which form part of this contract. Sums insured, limits,
deductibles, periods and percentages shown in square brackets are those stated
in the Schedule. An optional peril is covered only where the Schedule shows it
as agreed.


-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
PART 1 - PURPOSE AND KEY CONCEPTS
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

1.1 What this insurance does

Combined residential buildings insurance protects the policyholder against the
financial consequences of physical damage to their building. The perils that can
be insured are the ones bundled together in these conditions - fire, escape of
water, storm and hail, further natural hazards, and frost action on the external
surfaces among them. Which of the insurable perils are actually covered is agreed
between insurer and policyholder and recorded in the schedule.

Some perils are available as standard and one only on request. A peril of the
second kind attaches only where the schedule shows it as agreed; where it is not
agreed, the damage it would have answered for is outside the contract, and so is
everything done in consequence of that damage.

Where insured property is damaged by a covered peril, the insurer indemnifies the
cost of putting it back, in the same kind and quality and to the standard in
place before the loss. Two questions decide every item of a claim: what caused
the damage to the part worked on, and whether that part was itself damaged.
Neither question is answered by the trade that carried out the work, by the
account on which it appears, or by the occasion on which it was done.

1.2 How the wording is to be read

Personal designations are to be understood as gender-neutral throughout; no
parallel male and female forms are used.

1.3 Explanation of recurring terms (not legally binding)

Policyholder - the insurer's contracting party and the purchaser of the cover.

Insured event - the event for which the insurer pays. An event is an insured
event only where it is one of the perils described in Part 2 and shown in the
schedule as agreed, and where it acted on property insured under Part 4.

Exclusion - a peril, a type of damage or an item of property for which no cover
exists. Exclusions delimit what has been promised and keep the cover
calculable.

Affected part - a pipe, a fitting, a component, an elevation, a surface or a room
in which physical damage caused by an insured event is established by the loss
investigation. A part bearing damage of another origin is not an affected part,
whether that origin is weather, age, wear, want of maintenance or a cause that
cannot be established.

Pipework and fittings - the pipes of the water, drainage and heating systems
within the building, together with the valves, taps, connection elements,
flexible connectors, seals and comparable fittings incorporated in them.

External surface - the outer skin of the building and its finishes on any
elevation exposed to the weather: render, plaster, coatings, paint systems,
pointing, cladding, sealants and the substrate beneath them.

Leak location - the investigation carried out to establish where water is
escaping or where pipework has fractured, including the use of measuring,
imaging, acoustic, tracer or comparable technical equipment for that purpose, and
the opening up needed to reach the suspected place.

Access provision - the scaffolding, towers, platforms, lifting equipment,
protective sheeting and comparable arrangements erected so that work at height or
over an elevation can be carried out, together with their hire, erection and
dismantling.

Lump-sum item - a single price covering an identified body of work rather than a
separately itemised labour and material breakdown. A lump-sum item prices work;
it is assessed by the work it prices. It is to be distinguished from a charge
levied in addition to the work for administration, handling, coordination or
processing, which prices no work at all.

Ancillary charge - a charge that exists only because of a principal item of work:
the material consumed in it, the access provision for it, its transport, the
labour of carrying it out, and the attendance of the undertaking at the building.

Index-linked reinstatement cover with enhancement - a basis of cover that works
from the amount that would have to be spent to rebuild in the same kind and
quality, tracked against movements in building costs; that tracking affects both
the amount payable and the premium.

Duties - the things the policyholder must do or refrain from doing before,
during and after an insured event. Breaching a duty puts the cover at risk.

Secured lenders - creditors whose claim is secured by a charge registered
against the property. Their interests enjoy statutory protection: among other
things they must be brought into the process when insurance benefits are paid
out and when the contract is brought to an end.


-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
PART 2 - INSURED PERILS
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

2.1 The perils that can be covered

The insurer indemnifies insured property that is destroyed or damaged by, or
lost as a consequence of, the following events:

  (a) FIRE GROUP - fire; lightning strike; overvoltage caused by lightning;
      explosion; deflagration; implosion; impact or crash of an aircraft, its
      parts or its cargo; impact of a vehicle; scorching; smoke and soot.

  (b) ESCAPE OF WATER.

  (c) NATURAL HAZARDS, in two tiers:
        (c1) storm and hail;
        (c2) the further natural hazards - flood, backing-up of water,
             earthquake, ground subsidence, landslip, snow load, avalanche and
             volcanic eruption.

  (d) FROST ACTION ON EXTERNAL SURFACES, as defined in 2.6. This peril is
      optional; it exists only where the schedule shows it as agreed.

2.2 How the groups combine

Each of the groups (a), (b) and (c1) can be taken separately. The further natural
hazards under (c2) can only be taken in combination with one or more of the
perils in (a), (b) or (c1). Group (d) can be taken alongside any of the others;
it is never included by implication, and its absence does not narrow group (b).

2.3 The fire group defined

2.3.1 Fire
A fire is a combustion that has started without a hearth intended for it, or
that has escaped such a hearth, and that is capable of spreading under its own
power. Damage caused by a fire that developed out of a controlled, purposeful
fire is also covered.

2.3.2 Lightning strike
The direct passage of a lightning discharge onto property.

2.3.3 Overvoltage caused by lightning
Damage arising through overvoltage, overcurrent or short circuit, brought about
by a lightning discharge or by other atmospheric electricity, in insured
electrical installations and appliances.

2.3.4 Explosion and deflagration
Both are suddenly running force events resting on the tendency of gases or
vapours to expand. The two differ only in the intensity of that force.

An explosion of a vessel - a boiler, a pipe run and the like - is present only
under a further condition: the vessel wall must be torn open to such an extent
that a sudden equalisation of the pressure difference between the inside and the
outside occurs. Where an explosion inside a vessel is brought about by a chemical
reaction, tearing of the wall is not required.

2.3.5 Implosion
A sudden, unforeseen collapse of a hollow body under external overpressure
resulting from an internal underpressure.

2.3.6 Impact or crash of an aircraft
The impact or crash of an aircraft is covered, and equally the impact or crash of
its parts or its cargo.

2.3.7 Vehicle impact
The impact of a road, rail or water-borne vehicle against insured property is
covered, as is the impact of parts or cargo of such a vehicle. Consequential
damage to insured property arising from such an impact is covered.

Not covered is damage caused by a road or water-borne vehicle whose keeper or
driver is the policyholder or an occupant of the building.

Not covered is damage to means of transport, to their parts and cargo, and to
roads, drives and comparable trafficked surfaces.

2.3.8 Scorching
Scorch damage arising out of one of the events in 2.3.1 to 2.3.7 is covered.
Scorch damage from any other cause is covered up to [amount].

2.3.9 Smoke and soot
Smoke and soot damage arising out of one of the events in 2.3.1 to 2.3.8 is
covered.

Beyond that, damage is covered where smoke or soot directly damages or destroys
insured property, on condition that the smoke or soot escaped suddenly, and
contrary to intended operation, from a firing, heating, cooking or drying
installation situated on the insured site. Indemnity for this extension is capped
at [amount].

Not covered is damage arising from the gradual action of smoke or soot -
long-term surface soiling of the fogging type, for instance.

2.3.10 Damage excluded within the fire group
Not covered:
  (a) damage caused by earthquake, irrespective of any contributing causes;
  (b) damage to internal combustion engines caused by the explosions occurring
      inside the machine's combustion chamber, and damage arising at the
      switching elements of electrical switches through the gas pressure
      occurring inside them. Cover does exist, however, where such damage is the
      consequence of an insured fire event under 2.3.1.

2.4 Escape of water defined

2.4.1 The three headings
The escape of water peril covers three things: escape of water damage; fracture
damage to pipework inside buildings; and fracture damage to pipework outside
buildings.

2.4.2 Escape of water damage
Escaping water means water that has emerged contrary to its intended purpose
from:
  (a) pipes of the water supply, whether supply or drainage lines, or hoses
      connected to them;
  (b) other installations connected to those pipes or hoses, or the
      water-carrying parts of such installations;
  (c) heating or air-conditioning systems;
  (d) water-based extinguishing or sprinkler systems;
  (e) water beds or aquaria.

Operating fluids from heating or air-conditioning systems, and steam, also count
as escaping water. Fluids intended for the generation of energy do not.

Damage is also covered where it is caused by water that emerged, contrary to its
intended purpose, from rainwater drainage pipes running inside the building. For
this extension the exclusion of damage caused by precipitation (see 3.3(c)) does
not apply.

Water that reaches the building from outside - as precipitation, as run-off, as
splash, as wind-driven wetting of an elevation, or as moisture rising or
penetrating through the fabric from without - is not escaping water.

2.4.3 How far the escape of water damage extends
The indemnity extends to every part of the building that the escaping water
damaged, whichever side of the fabric that part lies on. An external surface is
covered under this heading where the escaping water reached it through the fabric
and damaged it; that it forms the outer skin of the building makes no difference,
and the optional peril in 2.1(d) is not needed for it.

Where escaping water within the meaning of 2.4.2 saturated a part of the fabric
and that saturation subsequently froze, the damage the freezing did to the
saturated part is damage caused by the escape of water. The intervening frost
does not displace the escape as the cause, and the fact that the same season's
weather was cold does not turn such damage into weather damage.

The policyholder must be able to show, by the pattern and the extent of the
damage or by a technical investigation, that the water in the fabric came from
the escape. Where the investigation shows the moisture to have entered from
outside, 2.6 and 3.5 apply instead.

2.4.4 Fracture damage to pipework inside buildings
Covered inside buildings:

  (a) frost-related and other fracture damage to pipes of
        - the water supply, whether supply or drainage lines, and the gas
          supply, or hoses connected to them;
        - heating or air-conditioning systems;
        - water-based extinguishing or sprinkler systems;
        - rainwater drainage.
      This presupposes that the pipes concerned are not a structural component of
      a boiler, a water heater or a comparable installation.

  (b) frost-related fracture damage to the following installations:
        - bath and shower fittings, washbasins, lavatories, taps and valves
          together with their connection hoses;
        - radiators, boilers, water heaters and comparable parts of heating or
          air-conditioning systems.

The whole structural body of the building, including the floor slab, counts as
"inside the building". Pipes of a solar heating installation on the roof count as
pipes inside the building. Unless something else has been agreed, pipes and
installations beneath the floor slab are not insured, whether load-bearing or
not.

Where a fitting, valve, connection element or flexible connector incorporated in
such pipework fractures through the action of frost, the fractured item and the
connection elements that have to be renewed with it are indemnified under 7.1.9,
together with the labour, the material consumed in the work and one attendance.

2.4.5 Fracture damage to pipework outside buildings
Covered outside buildings: frost-related and other fracture damage to supply
pipes of the water supply, or to pipes of heating or air-conditioning systems, in
each case insofar as the policyholder bears the risk for those pipes and insofar
as they either
  (a) serve the supply of insured buildings or installations, or
  (b) are situated on the insured site.

Indemnity for fracture damage to supply pipes that do not serve the supply of
insured buildings or installations, and for those not situated on the insured
site, is limited per insured event to the amounts agreed for those purposes.

2.4.6 Leak location
Where a fracture or an escape of water is established or reasonably suspected,
the insurer indemnifies the leak location within the meaning of 1.3 - including
the use of measuring or imaging equipment brought to the building for that
purpose, and the opening up needed to reach the suspected place - and the making
good of that opening up afterwards.

Leak location is indemnified even where the investigation shows the escape to
have been smaller than supposed. It is not indemnified where the investigation
shows the observed damage to have a cause that these conditions do not cover.

2.5 Natural hazards defined

2.5.1 Storm
Storm means a weather-driven movement of air reaching at least the gale threshold
on the recognised scale of wind strength, expressed as a defined minimum
sustained wind speed.

Where the wind strength at the loss location cannot be established, storm is
presumed if the policyholder demonstrates either of the following:
  (a) in the vicinity of the insured site the air movement caused damage to
      buildings that were in sound condition, or to other property of comparable
      resistance; or
  (b) given the sound condition of the insured building, the damage can only have
      arisen through storm.

2.5.2 Hail
Hail means solid precipitation in the form of grains of ice.

2.5.3 Which storm and hail events are covered
Only damage arising in one of the following ways is covered:
  (a) storm or hail acts directly on insured property, or on buildings in which
      insured property is located; consequential damage to insured property
      arising from this is covered;
  (b) storm or hail acts directly on buildings structurally joined to the insured
      building;
  (c) storm or hail acts directly on buildings structurally joined to buildings
      in which insured property is located;
  (d) storm or hail throws building parts, trees or other objects onto insured
      property, or onto buildings in which insured property is located;
      consequential damage to insured property arising from this is covered;
  (e) storm or hail throws building parts, trees or other objects onto buildings
      structurally joined to the insured building;
  (f) storm or hail throws building parts, trees or other objects onto buildings
      structurally joined to buildings in which insured property is located.

A single identifiable weather event of the strength described in 2.5.1 is
required. Repeated exposure to ordinary weather over a season or a number of
years is not such an event.

2.5.4 The further natural hazards

Flood
Flood means the inundation of the ground and soil of the insured site, or of
directly adjoining land, roads, footpaths or cycle paths, with substantial
quantities of surface water. It counts only where the inundation was caused by
  (a) the overflow of surface waters, standing or flowing,
  (b) precipitation, or
  (c) the emergence of groundwater at the surface as a consequence of (a) or (b).

Backing-up of water
Backing-up is present where water enters the building from the building's own
drainage pipes or from installations connected to them. It counts only where the
backing-up was caused by the overflow of surface waters, standing or flowing, or
by precipitation.

Earthquake
Earthquake means a naturally caused tremor of the ground triggered by geophysical
processes within the earth's interior. It is presumed on the conditions
corresponding to 2.5.1.

Ground subsidence
A naturally caused sinking of the ground above naturally formed cavities.

Landslip
A naturally caused sliding or falling away of masses of earth or rock.

Snow load
The effect of the weight of masses of snow or ice. Snow or ice masses sliding off
roofs also count as snow load.

Avalanche
Masses of snow or ice descending a mountain slope.

Volcanic eruption
A sudden release of pressure on the rupturing of the earth's crust, accompanied
by flows of lava, eruptions of ash, or the escape of other materials and gases.

2.6 Frost action on external surfaces

2.6.1 The peril
Where this peril is agreed, the insurer indemnifies external surfaces of the
insured building that are damaged by frost acting on them from without - by
freezing, by thawing, and by the repeated cycle of the two - so that the material
spalls, loses adhesion, delaminates, blows, cracks or otherwise fails.

2.6.2 What the indemnity comprises
Where this peril is agreed and an elevation has suffered such damage, the
indemnity comprises the making good of the damaged area: taking off the loosened
and failed material, preparing and re-forming the substrate beneath it, drying it
where drying is needed before the new work can proceed, priming it, applying the
finish system in the number of coats the system requires, the labour of the
tradespeople engaged, the access provision needed to reach the elevation, the
disposal of the removed material, and one attendance per undertaking.

2.6.3 What is not within the peril even where it is agreed
  (a) work on an elevation, or on a part of an elevation, that the frost did not
      damage - including recoating an undamaged area or an undamaged elevation so
      that the building presents a uniform appearance afterwards (7.1.5, 7.1.6);
  (b) an upgrade of the surface system beyond the standard in place before the
      loss (7.1.10);
  (c) damage arising from a cause other than frost acting on the surface - damp
      penetration, run-off, ageing, fatigue, shrinkage, settlement, loss of
      adhesion through age, defective original execution, or want of maintenance
      (3.1.4).

2.6.4 Where the peril is not agreed
Where the schedule does not show this peril as agreed, frost damage to an
external surface is not an insured event and 3.5 applies. This does not affect
2.4.3: an external surface damaged by water that escaped inside the building
remains covered under the escape of water peril whether or not the optional peril
was taken.


-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
PART 3 - EXCLUSIONS
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

3.1 General exclusions

3.1.1 War
Damage caused by war, warlike events, civil war, revolution, rebellion or
insurrection is not covered, irrespective of any contributing causes.

3.1.2 Civil commotion
Damage caused by internal civil unrest is not covered, irrespective of any
contributing causes.

3.1.3 Nuclear energy
Damage caused by nuclear energy, nuclear radiation or radioactive substances is
not covered, irrespective of any contributing causes.

3.1.4 Weathering, ageing and want of maintenance
Damage arising from the action of the weather on the building otherwise than
through a peril described in Part 2 and shown in the schedule as agreed is not
covered. This includes damage arising from rain, damp, wind-driven wetting and
standing moisture; from exposure, weathering, ageing, fatigue, shrinkage and
settlement cracking; from the gradual loss of adhesion or integrity of a
material; and from want of maintenance, deferred renewal or a defect in the
original execution or specification.

3.1.5 Perils not agreed
Damage brought about by a peril that the schedule does not show as agreed is not
covered, however the damage is described, whatever part it affects, and whether
or not the same notification also concerns covered damage.

3.2 Exclusions within the fire group

See 2.3.10.

3.3 Exclusions within the escape of water peril

Damage caused by the following is not covered, irrespective of any contributing
causes except where such causes are named below:
  (a) splash water or cleaning water;
  (b) dry rot and house-rot fungi of every kind;
  (c) groundwater, standing or flowing surface water, flood, precipitation, or a
      backing-up of water brought about by any of these causes;
  (d) earthquake, snow load, avalanche, volcanic eruption;
  (e) ground subsidence or landslip - unless escaping water within the meaning of
      2.4.2 caused the subsidence or the landslip;
  (f) fire; lightning strike; overvoltage caused by lightning; explosion;
      deflagration; implosion; impact or crash of an aircraft; vehicle impact;
      scorching; smoke and soot damage;
  (g) the opening of sprinklers or the operation of sprinkler nozzles on account
      of a fire, on account of pressure testing, or on account of alteration or
      repair work;
  (h) storm, hail.

The freezing of water that had already escaped within the meaning of 2.4.2 is not
one of these excluded causes; 2.4.3 second paragraph governs it.

Damage to buildings or parts of buildings that are not ready for occupation is
not covered. The same applies to property located in such buildings or parts of
buildings.

3.4 Exclusions within the natural hazards

Damage caused by the following is not covered, irrespective of any contributing
causes except where such causes are named below:
  (a) storm surge;
  (b) the penetration of rain, hail, snow or dirt through windows, external doors
      or other openings that were not properly closed. This exclusion does not
      apply where those openings were created by storm or hail and constitute
      damage to the building;
  (c) groundwater, except insofar as it emerged at the surface as a result of
      precipitation or of the overflow of surface waters;
  (d) fire; lightning strike; overvoltage caused by lightning; explosion;
      deflagration; implosion; impact or crash of an aircraft; vehicle impact;
      scorching; smoke and soot damage. This exclusion does not apply insofar as
      those perils were triggered by an insured earthquake;
  (e) drought or desiccation.

Damage to buildings and parts of buildings that are not ready for occupation, and
to property located within them, is not covered. Damage to shop windows and
display windows is likewise not covered.

3.5 External surfaces where the optional peril is not agreed

Where the schedule does not show the peril in 2.1(d) as agreed, the following are
not covered:
  (a) damage to an external surface caused by frost acting on it from without, or
      by any other cause falling under 3.1.4;
  (b) in consequence of (a), the taking off and renewal of loosened or failed
      surface material, the preparation, levelling and re-forming of the
      substrate beneath it, its drying, its priming, the successive coats of the
      new finish however many are applied, and any further work carried out on
      the elevation on the same occasion;
  (c) every ancillary charge attributable to (a) or (b) - the material consumed,
      the access provision, the labour, the attendance, the disposal of the
      removed material, and any lump-sum item pricing that work;
  (d) any upgrade of the surface system beyond the standard in place before the
      loss.

This applies whether the work is carried out at the same time as covered work, by
a further trade engaged on the same occasion, under the same commission, or on
the same or a separate account.

3.6 Site and establishment charges

Not covered, whichever trade levies them and whether the work they accompany is
covered or not:
  (a) provisioning, refreshment, catering and comparable subsistence for an
      undertaking's own personnel;
  (b) charges levied in addition to the work for administration, handling,
      coordination or processing;
  (c) an undertaking's own tools and consumable small equipment.
The equipment employed in leak location (2.4.6), the access provision under
7.1.8, the consumables actually used in covered work (7.1.7(e)) and a lump-sum
item pricing covered work (7.1.12) are not charges of this kind.

3.7 Work beyond the affected parts

Work carried out beyond those parts of the insured property that were themselves
affected by an insured event is not covered. Outlay that does not constitute a
repair or replacement cost is not indemnified. The delimitation is governed by
7.1.5 to 7.1.13.


-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
PART 4 - INSURED PROPERTY, INSURED LOCATION, DEDUCTIBLES
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

4.1 What is insured

Insured property comprises:
  (a) the buildings identified in the schedule;
  (b) their building components, including their pipework and fittings and their
      external surfaces;
  (c) their building accessories;
  (d) terraces on the insured site that directly adjoin the building;
  (e) further site installations.

That an item is insured property states which objects the cover can attach to. It
does not state that every kind of damage to that object is indemnified. What is
indemnified is damage caused by a peril shown in the schedule as agreed.

4.2 The categories defined

4.2.1 Building and dwelling
Buildings are structures connected to the ground. They must be capable of
affording protection against external influences and, for the purposes of these
conditions, must be intended for predominantly residential use.

Where the insured property is a self-contained dwelling within such a building,
these conditions apply to that dwelling and to those parts of the building that
constitute the policyholder's separate property, together with the policyholder's
share in the common parts.

4.2.2 Building components
Building components are items incorporated into a building that have lost their
independence through their firm connection with it. Fitted furniture and fitted
kitchens fall within this category where they were made individually for the
building and adapted to it with substantial installation effort. Add-on furniture
and add-on kitchens that are series-produced do not.

Also counting as building components are the fitting-out elements of the
dwelling: floor coverings together with their bedding, adhesive, underlay,
insulating and levelling layers; wall and ceiling finishes; interior doors; fixed
trim, beading and comparable edging elements; the pipework and fittings within
the meaning of 1.3; and the external surfaces within the meaning of 1.3.

4.2.3 Building accessories
Building accessories are movable items located inside the building or attached to
its exterior. They must serve the upkeep of the insured building or its
predominant intended purpose.

4.2.4 Terraces
Terraces are paved surfaces intended for occupation in the open air.

4.2.5 Further site installations
Further site installations means the items firmly connected with the ground and
soil of the insured site that are specified for that purpose in the schedule.

4.3 Property not insured

Not insured:
  (a) photovoltaic installations and their components - solar modules, mounting
      frames, fastening elements, inverters, module optimisers and the cabling.
      This extends to an electricity storage installation permanently connected
      to the photovoltaic installation and serving the supply of the building;
  (b) all items subsequently incorporated into the building by a tenant or by a
      condominium owner where that person both
        - procured or took the items over at their own expense, and
        - bears the risk for them.
      Where items are merely exchanged, the newly incorporated items are insured.
      Any different arrangement as to who bears the risk must be evidenced by the
      policyholder;
  (c) electronically stored data and programs. Costs of restoring electronically
      stored data and programs are covered only where this has been additionally
      agreed in the contract.

4.4 The insured location

The insured location is the insured site: the land parcel or parcels on which the
insured building stands. Where several buildings stand on one parcel, the insured
location is that part of the parcel which, by fencing or other demarcation,
belongs exclusively to the insured building or buildings.

4.5 Condominium and part-ownership units

4.5.1 Where the contract is with an association of condominium owners: if the
insurer is wholly or partly released from liability on account of the conduct of
individual condominium owners, it remains obliged to pay the remaining owners.
This applies to their separate property and to their shares in the common
property.

4.5.2 The co-ownership share of the owner against whom the insurer is wholly or
partly released is not indemnified, or is indemnified only in part.

The remaining condominium owners may nevertheless claim indemnity for that
co-ownership share. This presupposes that the additional indemnity is applied to
reinstating the common property. The condominium owner against whom the insurer
is wholly or partly released must reimburse the insurer for that additional
indemnity.

4.5.3 The two provisions above apply correspondingly to buildings insurance for
part-ownership units.

4.6 Deductibles

A deductible is the share of the indemnity, or the amount, that the policyholder
bears itself per insured event. Deductibles can be agreed individually and are
set out in the schedule. Where one event damages several parts of the building,
and where several trades are engaged in consequence of it, the deductible is
applied once. A deductible is applied only to an indemnity that is otherwise
payable; it does not create cover for damage of another origin.


-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
PART 5 - INSURED COSTS, LOSS OF RENT AND RENTAL VALUE
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

5.1 Which costs are covered

The insurer reimburses the following costs where they were necessary as a
consequence of an insured event and were actually incurred:
  (a) debris removal and disposal costs;
  (b) costs of leak location under 2.4.6;
  (c) costs of moving and protecting property;
  (d) costs of lost water, gas and heating oil, and of electricity lost from
      storage installations;
  (e) hotel costs.

Reimbursement of each head is limited to the amount agreed for it. The list is
exhaustive. Each head presupposes an insured event and relates only to property
that the event damaged.

5.2 The cost heads defined

5.2.1 Debris removal and disposal
Costs incurred in clearing away and demolishing insured property that an insured
event damaged, in taking away the material removed in the course of covered
repair work, and in disposing of an affected part that a covered replacement
takes the place of. This includes transporting the material to the nearest
disposal site, depositing it and destroying it.

It does not extend to the removal or disposal of material taken off a part of the
building whose damage is not covered; such removal is part of the work on that
part and follows it (7.1.11).

5.2.2 Leak location
Costs of the leak location within the meaning of 1.3 and 2.4.6, comprising the
attendance of the investigating undertaking, the labour, the use of the measuring
or imaging equipment employed, the opening up carried out to reach the suspected
place, and the making good of that opening up. Indemnity is capped at [amount]
per insured event.

5.2.3 Moving and protecting property
Costs incurred in moving, altering or protecting other property, reimbursable
where those measures serve to reinstate insured property damaged by an insured
event.

5.2.4 Lost water, gas, heating oil and stored electricity
Costs arising because water, gas or heating oil escaped contrary to its intended
purpose as a result of an insured event. Additional wastewater charges fall under
this head. Costs of electricity lost from storage installations are also
reimbursed. Indemnity is capped at [amount] per insured event.

5.2.5 Hotel costs
Costs of accommodation in a hotel or similar, excluding incidentals such as
breakfast. The precondition is that the dwelling permanently occupied by the
policyholder has become uninhabitable as a result of an insured event and that
confining themselves to a habitable part of it cannot reasonably be expected of
them.

Accommodation costs are reimbursed only where indemnity cannot be claimed under
another insurance contract, and only to the extent that they exceed the indemnity
payable for rental value under 7.5. Costs are reimbursed up to the point at which
the dwelling is habitable again, for a maximum of [number] days, capped at
[amount] per day.

5.3 Loss of rent and rental value

The insurer reimburses:
  (a) loss of rent, where tenants of residential premises have lawfully stopped
      paying rent in whole or in part, or have terminated the tenancy, on account
      of an insured event, including the running service charges in the sense of
      tenancy law;
  (b) the locally customary rental value of residential premises occupied by the
      policyholder itself, including those service charges, where on account of
      the insured event the policyholder cannot reasonably be expected to use at
      least parts of the dwelling;
  (c) any additional loss of rent or rental value caused by public-law
      restrictions on reinstatement.

5.4 The period for loss of rent and rental value

5.4.1 Loss of rent or rental value is reimbursed for the period during which the
rooms are unusable, but for no longer than [number] months from the occurrence of
the insured event.

5.4.2 It is reimbursed only to the extent that the policyholder has not culpably
delayed the resumption of use where resumption was possible. A delay attributable
to work that is not covered does not extend the period.

5.5 Commercially used premises

For commercially used premises, insurance of loss of rent or of the locally
customary rental value can be agreed.

5.6 Optionally insurable extensions

5.6.1 Where the tenant terminates the tenancy on account of the insured event and
the policyholder is unable to re-let the dwelling after completion of the works,
the insurer also reimburses that loss of rent, provided the policyholder was
unable to let the rooms at the time reinstatement was completed despite
exercising the care required in commerce. It applies until the rooms are re-let,
and at most until the end of the period under 5.4.

5.6.2 Where a tenancy cannot be entered into on account of the insured event, the
insurer reimburses the loss of rent from the contractually agreed start of the
tenancy until the end of the period under 5.4, provided the tenancy agreement had
already been concluded at the time of the insured event.


-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
PART 6 - BASIS OF COVER AND PREMIUM
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

6.1 Insurable value

The insurable value forms the basis for calculating the indemnity. The insurable
value determined for the building applies equally to building accessories,
terraces and further site installations as defined in 4.2.3 to 4.2.5.

6.2 Index-linked reinstatement value with enhancement

6.2.1 What is insured is the locally customary new-build value of the buildings
identified in the schedule, taken at the time of the insured event, in the
construction and finish standard existing at that time. Architects' fees and
other construction and planning costs form part of that value.

Where, within an insurance period, structural measures alter the area, the
building type, the construction or other agreed features underlying the premium
calculation, cover subsists until the end of that insurance period, even where
the measure taken increases value.

6.2.2 Two elements are built into the index-linked reinstatement value with
enhancement:

  - Additional costs arising from public-law restrictions on reinstatement, being
    the additional costs incurred because property affected by the loss cannot be
    reinstated in the same kind and quality on account of public-law
    requirements;

  - Price increases arising between the occurrence of the insured event and
    reinstatement initiated without delay.

6.2.3 The insurer tracks the cover under 6.2.1 against the development of
building costs (see 6.5). To that extent cover subsists on the basis of the
locally customary new-build value at the time of the reinstatement initiated
without delay after the insured event.

6.3 Index-linked current value with enhancement where reinstatement is omitted
    or delayed

For buildings that are not reinstated, or are reinstated late (see 7.6), only the
index-linked current value with enhancement is insured. That value is the
enhanced new-build value at the time of the insured event, less depreciation - in
particular depreciation for age and for the degree of wear.

6.4 Market value for permanently devalued buildings

For buildings designated for demolition, or otherwise permanently devalued, only
the achievable sale price excluding the land share is insured.

6.5 How the premium is calculated

The bases for calculating the premium are:
  (a) the area;
  (b) the building type;
  (c) the construction and the fit-out, including the external surface system;
  (d) the use;
  (e) the perils agreed, including any optional peril taken;
  (f) other agreed features material to the premium calculation; and
  (g) the adjustment factor.

The annual premium payable is calculated by multiplying together the number of
square metres of residential and usable floor area, the premium per square metre,
and the adjustment factor, plus the premium element attributable to (e).

6.6 Adjustment of cover and premium

6.6.1 Where cover is adjusted under 6.2.3, the premium changes accordingly, as
the adjustment factor rises or falls.

6.6.2 The adjustment factor changes with effect from 1 January of each year, for
the insurance period beginning in that year. It rises or falls in line with the
percentage by which the following two indices have moved:
  - a construction price index for residential buildings, taken for a defined
    reference month of the preceding year, and
  - a collectively agreed wage index for the construction sector, taken for a
    defined reference quarter of the preceding year.
Both indices are published by the competent national statistical authority.

In this adjustment the movement in the construction price index is weighted
[percentage] and the movement in the wage index [percentage]. When the
year-on-year rates of movement are calculated, and again when the two rates are
weighted, the result is rounded to two decimal places at each step. The
adjustment factor is rounded to two decimal places. In rounding, where the third
decimal place is a five or higher the figure is rounded up; otherwise it is
rounded down.

6.7 Subsequent change in a premium-rating feature

6.7.1 Premium increase
Where a circumstance under 6.5(a) to (f) subsequently changes and a higher
premium results, the insurer may demand the higher premium from the point at
which the change is notified. Taking up an optional peril, and upgrading the
external surface system, are changes of this kind. They take effect for the
future only and do not extend to an event that has already occurred.

6.7.2 Premium reduction
Where a circumstance under 6.5(a) to (f) subsequently ceases to apply and a lower
premium results, the insurer must reduce the premium from the point at which it
becomes aware of that. The same applies where such circumstances have lost their
significance, or where the policyholder had only mistakenly assumed that they
existed.


-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
PART 7 - CALCULATION AND PAYMENT OF THE INDEMNITY
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

7.1 Basis of calculation

7.1.1 The insurer reimburses:

  (a) for destroyed buildings - the locally customary reinstatement costs under
      6.2.1, taken at the time of the insured event, including the additional
      costs under 6.2.2;

  (b) for damaged buildings, damaged pipework and fittings, damaged external
      surfaces and other damaged insured property - the necessary repair costs at
      the time of the insured event, including the restoration of the finish of
      the affected area. The insurer additionally compensates any diminution in
      value that the repair does not offset. Reimbursement is capped at the
      insurable value at the time of the insured event;

  (c) for destroyed insured property, and for an affected part that can no longer
      be repaired - the cost of a replacement of the same kind, quality and
      specification, determined under 7.1.9.

Every head of this Part presupposes an insured event within the meaning of 1.3.

7.1.2 Where technically still usable substance may not be used for reinstatement
because of public-law requirements, the policyholder receives corresponding
indemnity under 7.1.1, provided either that the official orders in question were
not issued before the insured event occurred, or that use of the property was not
already wholly or partly prohibited at that time.

7.1.3 Price increases occurring between the insured event and reinstatement are
indemnified where reinstatement is secured within three years of the occurrence
of the insured event.

7.1.4 The achievable sale price of remains is set off in calculating the
indemnity under 7.1.1.

7.1.5 Extent of the repair
Indemnity is confined to those parts of the insured property that were themselves
affected by the insured event, and within an elevation or a surface to the area
in which damage caused by the event is established.

Work carried out on a part, an area, an elevation or a room that was not itself
affected is not covered. This applies even where the work is carried out
  (a) so that treated and untreated areas correspond in appearance, colour,
      texture, pattern or material;
  (b) for reasons of convenience, or because treating a whole elevation is more
      economical than treating the affected area of it;
  (c) at the same time as covered work, in the course of it, or as part of the
      same overall project;
  (d) by the same undertaking as the covered work, or by a further trade engaged
      on the same occasion, and invoiced together with it.

Where the damage claimed on a part of the building has an origin that is not
covered, that part is not an affected part, however close it may be in time or
place to covered damage, and however plainly it needs attention.

7.1.6 Continuous surfaces
Where only part of a single continuous surface was affected, indemnity extends to
the cost of treating the adjoining unaffected sections of that same surface only
where a replacement material corresponding to the original is no longer
obtainable and a visible discontinuity would otherwise remain. It does not extend
to a separate elevation, and it does not apply where the adjoining sections bear
damage of an origin that is not covered.

7.1.7 Preparatory and ancillary work
The necessary repair costs under 7.1.1(b) include:
  (a) taking down, dismantling and removing the affected components and finishes;
  (b) the opening up needed to reach the affected part, and the making good of
      that opening up afterwards;
  (c) the drying and moisture-removal measures necessary before the repair of an
      affected part can be carried out, and the preparation, levelling and
      re-forming of the substrate before a new finish is applied to it;
  (d) materials of a type, quality, grade and specification corresponding to
      those in place immediately before the insured event, and the number of
      coats that the specified finish system requires;
  (e) the auxiliary material, sealing material, fixings, cleaning material and
      comparable consumables actually used in carrying out the covered work;
  (f) the labour of the tradespeople engaged on the covered work, at their
      respective rates.

Each of these heads exists only in respect of an affected part. Applied to a part
whose damage is not covered, none of them is indemnified.

7.1.8 Access provision
Where covered work cannot be carried out without an access provision within the
meaning of 1.3, its hire, erection and dismantling are a repair cost and are
indemnified. Where the access provision serves both covered and non-covered work,
it is apportioned; where it serves only non-covered work, it is not indemnified.
An access provision retained beyond the period needed for the covered work is
indemnified only for that period.

7.1.9 Renewal of a fractured pipe or fitting
Where a pipe or a fitting has fractured in an insured event, the indemnity
comprises the fractured item, the connection elements and seals that have to be
renewed with it, the labour under 7.1.7(f), the consumables under 7.1.7(e), the
opening up and making good under 7.1.7(b), and one attendance under 7.1.11.
Renewal is on a like-for-like basis; 7.1.10 applies to any higher specification
chosen.

7.1.10 No improvement on the pre-loss standard
Reinstatement proceeds on the basis of the type, quality, grade, build-up and
specification in place immediately before the insured event. Where a system of
higher specification, greater thickness, added function or premium range is
chosen instead, indemnity is limited to the cost of an equivalent replacement
corresponding to what was in place before the loss; the difference is borne by
the policyholder.

Where the principal work to which such an upgrade relates is not covered at all,
the upgrade is not covered either, and the question of a difference in cost does
not arise.

7.1.11 Ancillary charges and attendance
An ancillary charge within the meaning of 1.3 is indemnified only to the extent
that the principal item of work to which it relates is itself indemnified. Where
the principal item is not covered, the labour, the material consumed in it, the
access provision for it, the disposal of what it removed and the attendance for
it are not covered either, however designated, whichever trade levies them, and
whether they appear on the same account as covered work or on a separate one.

One attendance per undertaking per insured event is indemnified, provided that
work indemnified under these conditions was carried out at that attendance. A
further or return visit by the same undertaking in respect of the same insured
event is not separately indemnified, whatever the reason for it and however
designated, unless the insurer agreed to it in advance.

7.1.12 Lump-sum items and charges levied in addition to the work
A lump-sum item within the meaning of 1.3 is indemnified where the work it prices
is covered work carried out on an affected part. Where it prices work that is not
covered, it is not indemnified; where it prices both, it is apportioned, and if it
cannot be apportioned from the information supplied the insurer may require an
itemised account before determining the claim.

A charge that prices no work - one levied in addition to the itemised or
lump-sum work for administration, handling, coordination or processing - is not
indemnified, whether or not the work it accompanies is covered (3.6(b)). The same
applies to provisioning for an undertaking's own personnel and to its own tools
and small equipment (3.6(a), (c)).

7.1.13 Assessment item by item and trade by trade
Each item claimed is assessed on its own merits, and each trade's account is
assessed in the same way. That covered work was carried out by one trade does not
carry the work of another; that two trades attended in respect of the same
notification does not make the second trade's work an insured loss, nor does it
make it a non-covered one.

Where an item is presented as a single combined line, it is assessed by its
predominant stated purpose; where that purpose is work on a part whose damage is
not covered, the whole line falls, including the preparation, the finish, the
labour and the ancillary charges bundled into it.

7.2 Market value

Insofar as a building is designated for demolition or otherwise permanently
devalued, insured property is indemnified at the achievable sale price excluding
the land share.

7.3 Construction specification lower or higher than described

7.3.1 Where the insured buildings, in their actual specification at the time of
the insured event, are of lower value than described in the contract, the insurer
is not obliged to compensate more than the loss actually incurred, measured at
the locally customary new-build value.

7.3.2 Where the actual specification at the time of the insured event is of
higher value, this can lead to a reduction of the indemnity. The basis is then
the specification described in the contract (see 6.5(a) to (f)), and the insurer
reimburses only the reinstatement costs (7.1.1(a)) or the necessary repair costs
(7.1.1(b)) for that specification.

The following remain unaffected: the scope and adjustment of cover (Part 6);
breach of the pre-contractual duty of disclosure under the general contract
provisions; and increase in risk (9.4).

7.4 Costs

Insured costs under Part 5 are reimbursed where it is demonstrated that they were
actually incurred, subject to the agreed limits. A cost falling outside the
exhaustive list in 5.1, and not being a repair cost under this Part, is not
reimbursed.

7.5 Loss of rent and rental value

The insurer reimburses the insured loss of rent or rental value up to the end of
the agreed period under 5.4.

7.6 The reinstatement element of the indemnity

The policyholder acquires a claim to payment of that part of the indemnity which
exceeds the current-value loss - the reinstatement element - only where
  (a) the policyholder ensures that it will use the indemnity to reinstate
      insured property of the same kind and intended purpose at the previous
      location; and
  (b) the reinstatement is secured within three years of the occurrence of the
      insured event.

Applying the indemnity to work that is not covered does not satisfy condition
(a). Where reinstatement at the previous location is legally impossible or cannot
be justified economically, it is sufficient to erect the building at another
location within the same country. The policyholder must repay the reinstatement
element where, through its own fault, the property was not reinstated within a
reasonable period.

7.7 Value added tax

Value added tax is reimbursed only if and to the extent that it was actually
incurred on the occasion of the reinstatement. It is not reimbursed where the
policyholder is entitled to recover input tax. Tax charged on an item that is not
indemnified is not indemnified either.

7.8 Deductible

Deductibles are deducted from the indemnity in the amount agreed, once per
insured event, across all trades engaged in consequence of that event.

7.9 When the indemnity falls due

7.9.1 The indemnity falls due once the insurer has conclusively determined the
claim as to its basis and its amount. One month after notifying the loss, the
policyholder may claim as an interim payment the amount that is, on the
prevailing assessment, payable as a minimum.

7.9.2 That part of the indemnity which goes beyond the current-value loss falls
due once the policyholder has demonstrated that it has secured the reinstatement.

7.10 Repayment of the reinstatement element

The policyholder is obliged to repay indemnity paid under 7.9.2 where, through
its own fault, the property was not reinstated within a reasonable period. This
extends to any interest the insurer has paid under 7.11.2.

7.11 Interest

Insofar as no more extensive obligation to pay interest arises on another legal
basis:

7.11.1 The indemnity bears interest from the notification of the loss, save
insofar as it was paid within one month.

7.11.2 That part of the indemnity which goes beyond the current-value loss bears
interest from the point at which the policyholder demonstrated that it has
secured the reinstatement.

7.11.3 The interest rate is [number] percentage point(s) below the applicable
statutory base rate of interest, but at least [percentage] and at most
[percentage] per year. Interest falls due together with the indemnity.

7.12 Suspension of time limits

In calculating the periods under 7.9, 7.11.1 and 7.11.2, any period during which
the indemnity cannot be determined or cannot be paid owing to the fault of the
policyholder is left out of account.

7.13 Deferral of payment

The insurer may defer payment for as long as:
  (a) there is doubt as to the policyholder's entitlement to receive payment;
  (b) official or criminal proceedings against the policyholder or its
      representative arising out of this insured event are still pending;
  (c) a legally required involvement of a secured lender has not taken place.


-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
PART 8 - EXPERT DETERMINATION PROCEDURE
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

8.1 Determining the amount of the loss

After an insured event has occurred, the policyholder may require that the amount
of the loss be determined in an expert determination procedure. Insurer and
policyholder may also agree on such a procedure jointly.

8.2 Further determinations

Policyholder and insurer may agree to extend the procedure to further
determinations relating to the insured event, including which parts of the
building the event damaged, the origin of damage found elsewhere on the building,
and in particular whether moisture found in an elevation came from within the
building or from without. The procedure determines the amount of the loss; it
cannot bring within the cover a peril that the schedule does not show as agreed.

8.3 Procedure before the determination

8.3.1 Each party is to nominate one expert in text form - by email, fax or letter,
for example. A party that has nominated its expert may call on the other party in
text form to nominate the second expert; in doing so it must name the expert it
has itself nominated. The second expert must be nominated within two weeks of
receipt of that request. If that does not happen, the requesting party may have
the expert appointed by the court with local jurisdiction for the loss location.
Where the insurer makes the request, it must draw the policyholder's attention to
this consequence.

8.3.2 The insurer may not nominate as expert:
  (a) competitors of the policyholder;
  (b) persons standing in a permanent business relationship with the
      policyholder;
  (c) persons employed by competitors or business partners of the policyholder,
      or standing in a comparable relationship with them.

8.3.3 Before beginning their determinations, the two experts nominate in text
form a third expert as umpire. The restriction in 8.3.2 applies to that
nomination as well. If the experts cannot agree, the umpire is appointed by the
court with local jurisdiction for the loss location, on the application of either
party.

8.4 Content of the determination

The experts' findings must state:
  (a) a schedule of the destroyed and the damaged insured property, together with
      the corresponding insurable values at the time of the insured event,
      distinguishing damage caused by the insured event from damage of another
      origin, and the affected areas of an elevation from the unaffected ones;
  (b) the reinstatement and repair costs;
  (c) the residual values of the property affected by the loss;
  (d) the insured costs and the insured loss of rent or rental value.

8.5 Procedure after the determination

Each expert transmits its findings to both parties simultaneously. Where the two
sets of findings diverge, the insurer passes them to the umpire without delay.
The umpire decides the points that remain in dispute; the experts' findings form
the limits of the umpire's scope for decision. The umpire transmits its decision
to both parties simultaneously.

The findings of the experts, or of the umpire, are binding on the contracting
parties. They are not binding where it is demonstrated that they manifestly
deviate substantially from the true state of affairs. The insurer calculates the
indemnity on the basis of binding findings.

Where the findings are not binding, the court makes a binding determination. The
same applies where the experts cannot or will not make the determination, or
where they delay it.

8.6 Costs

Unless something else has been agreed, each party bears the costs of its own
expert. The costs of the umpire are borne by the two parties in equal shares.

8.7 Duties remain unaffected

The expert determination procedure does not affect the policyholder's duties.


-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
PART 9 - POLICYHOLDER DUTIES AND INCREASE IN RISK
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

9.1 Contractually agreed safety requirements before an insured event

9.1.1 Insured property must be kept in proper condition at all times. This
applies in particular to water-carrying installations and equipment, to roofs, to
the external surfaces of the building and their coatings, and to items attached
to the exterior. Defects or damage to such property must be remedied without
delay. Keeping the external surfaces weathertight and sound is a matter of
upkeep.

9.1.2 Buildings or parts of buildings that are not in use must be inspected
sufficiently frequently at every time of year. In addition, all water-carrying
installations and equipment there must be shut off, drained, and kept drained.

9.1.3 During the cold season all buildings and parts of buildings must be heated,
and this must be checked sufficiently frequently. Alternatively, all
water-carrying installations and equipment there must be shut off, drained, and
kept drained.

9.1.4 To avoid flood and backing-up damage:
  (a) in rooms at risk of backing-up, backflow prevention devices must be kept
      operational;
  (b) the drainage lines on the insured site must be kept clear.

9.2 Duties after an insured event

9.2.1 The policyholder must avert and mitigate the loss so far as it reasonably
can, and must shut off the supply and arrange for the leak to be located without
undue delay.

9.2.2 The replaced items, and the affected areas, must be kept available for
inspection until the claim has been determined, unless the insurer releases them
earlier.

9.3 Consequences of a breach of duty

Where the policyholder breaches one of the duties in 9.1 or 9.2, the following
applies, subject to the conditions set out in the general contract provisions:
the insurer is entitled to terminate the contract. It may also be wholly or
partly released from liability.

9.4 Circumstances constituting an increase in risk

An increase in risk subject to notification may exist in particular where:
  (a) a circumstance changes about which the insurer asked before the contract
      was concluded;
  (b) the building, or the predominant part of it, is no longer in use;
  (c) construction work is carried out on the building in the course of which the
      roof is wholly or partly removed;
  (d) construction work on the building renders it predominantly unusable;
  (e) a commercial operation is taken up or changed within the building;
  (f) the building is placed under heritage protection after conclusion of the
      contract;
  (g) the external surface system is changed for one of a materially different
      build-up.

9.5 Consequences of an increase in risk

The consequences of an increase in risk are governed by the general contract
provisions.

9.6 Claims presentation

Each item claimed must be presented in such a way that it can be allocated to a
peril shown in the schedule as agreed, to a part of the building that the peril
damaged, and to a head of indemnity under Part 5 or Part 7. The claim must state,
for each part of the building on which work is claimed, what damaged it; where
moisture in an elevation is in question, it must state whether the moisture came
from within the building or from without.

Where accounts from more than one trade are submitted in respect of one
notification, each is assessed separately under 7.1.13. Where an account covers
both covered and non-covered work, the two must be separated, and any lump-sum
item or access provision relating to both must be presented so that it can be
apportioned. An item that cannot be allocated to a part damaged by an insured
event is declined - the material, the preparation, the drying, the finish, the
labour, the disposal and any lump sum alike.


-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
PART 10 - CANCELLATION, SECURED LENDERS, TRANSFER OF OWNERSHIP
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

10.1 Cancellation where a security right has been registered

Where a secured lender has registered its charge over the property, cancellation
of the insurance relationship by the policyholder in respect of the fire peril
group - fire; lightning strike; overvoltage caused by lightning; explosion;
deflagration; implosion; impact or crash of an aircraft; vehicle impact;
scorching; smoke and soot damage - is effective only in the following cases:

10.1.1 the policyholder demonstrated, at least one month before expiry of the
insurance contract, that at the point in time at which the cancellation was at
the latest permissible the property was no longer encumbered with the charge; or

10.1.2 the policyholder demonstrated, at least one month before expiry of the
insurance contract, that the secured lender consented to the cancellation.

This does not apply to a cancellation following a disposal of the property, or to
a cancellation in the insured event.

10.2 Legal position following a transfer of ownership

10.2.1 Where the policyholder disposes of the insured property, the acquirer
steps into its place in the insurance contract. This happens at the time of the
transfer of ownership; in the case of real property, at the date of registration
in the land register. From that time the acquirer takes over the rights and
obligations of the policyholder under the insurance relationship.

10.2.2 Seller and acquirer are jointly and severally liable for the premium for
the insurance period in which the transfer of ownership occurs.

10.2.3 The insurer need only recognise the acquirer's entry into the insurance
contract once it becomes aware of that entry.

10.3 Rights of cancellation on a transfer of ownership

10.3.1 The insurer is entitled to cancel the insurance contract as against the
acquirer, observing a notice period of one month. This right lapses if the
insurer does not exercise it within one month of becoming aware of the disposal.

10.3.2 The acquirer is entitled to cancel the insurance contract with immediate
effect, or with effect from the end of the current insurance period, in text form
- by email, fax or letter, for example. That right lapses if the acquirer does
not exercise it within one month of the acquisition. Where the acquirer is
unaware that the insurance exists, the right lapses one month after the acquirer
becomes aware of it.

10.3.3 In the event of a cancellation under 10.3.1 or 10.3.2, the seller alone
remains liable for payment of the premium.

10.4 Duties of notification

10.4.1 The disposal must be notified to the insurer without delay, in text form,
by the seller or by the acquirer.

10.4.2 Where that notification has been omitted, the insurer is not obliged to
pay in the insured event. This applies only where both of the following
conditions are met:
  - the insured event occurred later than one month after the point at which the
    notification ought to have been received by the insurer; and
  - the insurer demonstrates that it would not have concluded the existing
    contract with the acquirer.

10.4.3 By way of departure from 10.4.2, the insurer is obliged to pay where
  - it was aware of the disposal at the point in time at which the notification
    ought to have been received by it; or
  - at the time of the insured event the period for the insurer's cancellation
    had already expired and it had not cancelled.

===============================================================================
END OF DOCUMENT

case.description:
Buildings frost claim after a prolonged deep freeze. Two separate things happened. Inside, a water fitting failed in the cold and had to be repaired, with a thermal imaging camera used to find where the escape was before opening up.

Outside, and unrelated to the internal fitting, the exterior render simply could not take the freeze-thaw cycling. The plaster cracked, blew and fell off the facade under the cold acting on it from the outside. No internal water reached that render; it was the outdoor temperature working on the wall surface.

For the file: the owner is not putting the plain render back as it was. The facade is being redone in a premium insulated render system, a clear upgrade on the old plain plaster, and the crew are taking the new finish across elevations that had not lost any render.
